passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Thank you for standing by. Good day, everyone, and welcome to The Boeing Company's Third Quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. Please be advised that today's call is being recorded. The management discussion and slide presentation, plus the analyst Q&A session, are being broadcast live over the Internet. To ask a question on today's call, please press *1 on your telephone. At this time, I am turning the call over to Mr. Eric Hill, Vice President of Investor Relations, for opening remarks and introductions. Mr. Hill, please go ahead.

passages.heading: Eric Hill, Vice President of Investor Relations
passages.text: Eric Hill, Vice President of Investor Relations: Thank you, and good morning. Welcome to Boeing's quarterly earnings call. With me today are Robert K. Ortberg, Boeing's President and Chief Executive Officer, and Jesus Malave, Boeing's Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. This quarter's webcast earnings release and presentation, which include relevant disclosures and non-GAAP reconciliations, are available on our website. Today's discussion includes forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties, including the ones described in our SEC filings. As always, we will leave time at the end of the call for analyst questions. With that, I will turn the call over to Robert K. Ortberg.

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: Well, thanks, Eric, and good morning, everyone. Thanks for joining today's call. As we enter the final months of the year, we are continuing to make progress across our businesses, having completed many of the key milestones in our 2026 plan and building on the trust we have restored with our stakeholders. Through the third quarter, we delivered 161 commercial aircraft, the most since 2018. We received FAA certification for the 737-7 in July and the 737-10 just last week. We reached a new four-year agreement with the union representing our engineering and technical workforce in the Pacific Northwest, avoiding any work interruption. And we secured major program awards across our defense and space portfolio, including multibillion-dollar contracts on key programs like the PAC-3 and the F-15EX. And we scored a generational win with the U.S. Navy: they selected Boeing to design, build, and deliver its sixth-generation fighter jet, making Boeing the exclusive sixth-generation fighter company for both the U.S. Air Force and the U.S. Navy. These accomplishments reflect the significant progress we are making, and they are made possible by the sustained focus of our team on safety, quality, and performance. We know there is more work to do, and I have said before, our progress is not always going to be perfectly linear. But we continue to improve, and I am confident we are on the right track. I will touch on the highlights I

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: just shared, as well as areas that require more attention in the quarters ahead. Let's start with our development programs. All year, we have said that certifying our new aircraft models is one of our most important goals. The FAA certification of the 737-7 and the -10 represents the culmination of nearly 100 test flights and more than 4,000 hours of ground and flight testing. I want to thank our employees who worked on or supported these programs and never lost sight of our mission. And to our customers and partners, I extend my gratitude for the steadfast support and confidence in these airplanes. We look forward to the newest members of the 737 MAX family delivering on their promise of greater efficiency and more capability. With the 737-7 and -10 FAA certifications complete, our focus now centers squarely on the 777-9. We continue to make progress on flight testing and still need approval to begin the balance of the flight-test program, including ETOPS testing. We continue to expect first delivery in 2027, and all of our latest assumptions continue to be within the EAC we reset last year. Turning now to our commercial factories. On the 737, we continue to work towards stabilizing production at 47 airplanes per month. Our factory's key performance indicators are performing well, particularly in final assembly, where we have seen a 40% improvement in rework since the start of last year. However, as I mentioned at a conference last month, it is taking us longer than we had

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: expected to demonstrate performance at rate 47. We are making progress, but we still have more work to do, and I am expecting it will take us into next year to get fully stable at this rate. Our output of wings is improving, but we need to demonstrate sustained performance at this level and ensure we have a high-confidence plan to step up to rate 52 when the system is ready. To reach 52 aircraft per month, we have to get the North Line certified and producing, our back shops, including wings, stable and ready, and fuselages in Wichita stable at the higher rates. Taken together, and integrating our learning from this year, our financial plan will target rate 52 in the back half of 2027. As I have said many times before, it is more important that we do this ramp right than in what particular month we achieve a rate break. We will stay disciplined here. Switching now to the 787. We are stable at eight aircraft per month, and the factory is performing well. While we have stability in our factory, delivery cadence has been uneven month to month due to the seat certification challenges we have discussed previously. We are seeing increased stability in our supply chain and closely watching engine delivery performance, as it remains the pacing item for rate 10. We still expect to start the transition to 10 per month yet this year, and we are making good progress on our Charleston expansion to support even higher production rates. Beyond the progress we are making in our factories,

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: we are also continuing to position Boeing for the long term. That is showing up in the quality of our backlog, the demand we are seeing across the portfolio, and in the investments and program wins that position us well into the future. Last month, we achieved a transformational win that will shape the company for decades to come when the U.S. Navy selected Boeing as the winner of the F/A-XX competition. To be selected for another sixth-generation fighter program is a testament to our innovation, our team, and the trust we have built with our customers. It is a true honor to support the national security priorities, and a responsibility we take very seriously. In addition to F/A-XX, we continue to see strong demand for proven franchises across our defense and space portfolio. Boeing received a seven-year contract to accelerate and eventually triple the PAC-3 Seeker production, supported by our early investments in facilities, workforce, and supply chain. In the quarter, we also received a contract to manufacture 22 more F-15EX aircraft for the U.S. Air Force. This award brings the total number of aircraft under contract to 120, with the potential for additional upside as the F-15EX continues to demonstrate the value of its unmatched payload and range capability. Beyond new franchise wins, we also continue to see tangible benefits from the active management approach we have talked about. As I said last quarter, Starliner was a program where we still had work to do with the

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: customer. We have since worked with NASA on a path forward to support future flights while reducing our program risks, including $359 million of additional NASA funding. Taken together, these are the kinds of actions and outcomes that will support our customers, strengthen Boeing, and position us well for the future. That long-term position is also beginning to give us greater visibility into the financial path forward. As I mentioned, over the last two years, we have made exceptional progress restoring trust, retiring risk, transforming our culture, and rebuilding the foundation of safety and quality that will help ensure durable success. We have also been deliberate about not getting ahead of ourselves, given the range of outcomes tied to the production ramp, certification timing, and other critical program execution. But we appreciate that it has been difficult for shareowners to assess how our progress will translate into financial performance. We are now at a point where the range of outcomes is narrowing. As we look ahead, our outlook is supported by a record backlog of $745 billion with improved pricing dynamics, a more stable production system, better underwriting on development programs, and our plans for continued progress on aircraft certification. Taken together, those factors give us confidence to share a multiyear free cash flow target for the business. We have narrowed our range and expect to generate approximately $2 billion of free cash flow in 2026. I am

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: expecting that will improve to about $3 billion in 2027, inclusive of the additional CapEx to support the F/A-XX development. We believe this should improve to about $6 billion in 2028 as we start to burn off some of the headwinds and accelerate from there. I expect to achieve the $10 billion target in 2029. Jesus will provide further color on the elements driving this trajectory in his remarks, but it is important to highlight that we continue to see significant growth potential beyond $10 billion, in line with our prior comments. To sum it up, we remain well positioned for the long term. I am pleased with the progress we have made so far. We have come a long way, but we are entering a new phase, and the bar is higher now, as it should be. Our job is to keep raising our performance to meet higher expectations while always prioritizing safety, quality, and stability. I am confident we will get there because we are doing the right work and taking the right actions to build more durable, dependable performance over time. Before I close, I want to thank all of our employees for the work they are doing every day to move Boeing forward. With that, I will turn it over to Jesus to discuss our financial results in more detail before we move to Q&A.

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: Thanks, Robert, and good morning, everyone. Starting with consolidated financial results for the quarter, revenue of $24.2 billion was up 4%, primarily driven by higher defense and services volume, partially offset by less favorable commercial delivery mix in the quarter. Operating margin improved to 1.5%, and core earnings per share improved to a loss of $0.34, reflecting higher segment earnings and lower corporate expenses. Free cash flow was positive $464 million in the quarter, an improvement versus the prior year, driven by improved working capital, partially offset by approximately $700 million of Department of Justice settlement payments and planned CapEx for our investments to expand capacity in Charleston and St. Louis. Turning to BCA on the next page. BCA delivered 161 airplanes in the quarter. Revenue was $10.7 billion, down 3% year over year, driven primarily by less favorable delivery mix. Operating margin of negative 6.5% improved materially versus the prior year's results, which were impacted by the 777X charge. That improvement was partially offset by a reduction in booking rates associated with production rate adjustments and higher estimated supply chain costs. Backlog at BCA increased again to a new record level of $612 billion. It includes over 6,300 airplanes. This includes orders during the quarter from Turkish Airlines, Ethiopian Airlines, and Lufthansa. Drilling down on commercial

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: program performance, starting with the 737, we delivered 124 airplanes in the quarter. As we close out the year, the delay in stability at 47 per month is expected to translate to lower delivery output and come in shy of the 500-delivery target. Let me remind you that we have built -7 and -10 aircraft prior to certification that will start delivering early next year. Going forward, we expect longer intervals between rate steps the higher we go, which is more in line with our historically demonstrated performance. That said, our team has detailed plans for what is required to get to higher rates, and we continue to make investments to create more capacity and resiliency in our production system that will enable stronger performance at higher levels, with a consistent focus on safety and quality. On the 787, we delivered 22 airplanes in the quarter. We continue to expect to deliver 90 to 100 airplanes in the year, but expect it to be closer to the lower end given the delays in getting to rate 10. In Charleston, our factory expansion is underway, and we expect the majority of the capability to come online late next year. In addition to the two lines in our current footprint, our second final-assembly building will add a third line that increases capacity, flexibility, and resiliency in our production system. On the current 777 metal-wing freighter, we received FAA approval for incremental production of up to 35 units, further extending the most popular dedicated freighter of

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: all time. During the quarter, our 777 freighter and 767 tanker production lines were disrupted by a supplier of wing components. Shipments from that supplier have resumed. However, there will be a gap in our production system that gradually flows through these production lines over the next few quarters. The cost of that disruption was not material in the third quarter, but will be treated as abnormal cost and period expense over the next few quarters. Finally, on 777X, as Robert mentioned, we remain on track for first delivery in 2027. As we get closer to certification, we have firmed up our production and delivery plan. We are currently producing airplanes at a rate of approximately one per month and expect to stay at that level for most of 2027. These latest assumptions are within our EAC. With respect to program cash flow, we continue to expect 2027 to be a significant use of cash, with 2028 improving before turning positive in 2029. Like the rest of our programs, we are prioritizing safety, quality, and stability as we ramp this new production system and work towards a delivery schedule that our customers can reliably plan for. Let's shift over to BDS on the next page. BDS delivered 30 aircraft and three satellites in the quarter. Revenue increased 15% to $7.9 billion, driven primarily by higher volume, including growth on classified programs in missiles and weapons. Spirit contributed approximately $150 million of sales in the quarter, or two points of growth. BDS

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: operating margin was 6.2% in the quarter and includes a $252 million gain on the sale of HRL Laboratories. Across the BDS portfolio, we continue to see operating performance gains in line with our expectations of steady margin improvement, and we remain confident in our path to high-single-digit operating margins by the end of the decade. BDS booked $23 billion in orders during the quarter, with a record backlog of $101 billion. We remain committed to our strategy of entering into appropriate contract structures on new business. Importantly, in the quarter, BDS was selected by the U.S. Navy to design, build, and deliver the F/A-XX next-generation fighter aircraft. This order was not included in our third-quarter backlog, pending completion of the source selection and evaluation process. Now moving to Global Services on the next page. BGS sustained its momentum and delivered another quarter of strong financial performance. Revenue was up 4% to $5.6 billion. Excluding the impact of the digital aviation solutions divestiture, revenue was up 11% over the prior year, primarily driven by government and commercial modifications volume. Operating margin of 18.3% was up from the prior year, on favorable volume and mix, partially offset by the divestiture last year. Both commercial and government businesses delivered double-digit margins in the quarter. Operationally, the BGS team continues to demonstrate process improvements across the business. For example, on the C-17 heavy

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: maintenance program, they continue to perform work at record-low rework levels while taking on greater scope of work for our customer, supporting revenue growth and margin performance. BGS received $5 billion of orders and ended the quarter with a backlog of $33 billion. Shifting over to cash and debt. Cash and marketable securities ended at $20.7 billion, primarily reflecting cash flow generated in the quarter. The debt balance was unchanged from the prior quarter at $45.9 billion. We continue to maintain access to $10 billion of revolving credit facilities, all of which remain undrawn. We remain committed to strengthening the balance sheet and supporting our investment-grade rating. Now let me provide some additional context on our free cash flow outlook and targets. First, as Robert noted, we have narrowed our prior range and expect to deliver approximately $2 billion of free cash flow in 2026. This includes the assumption of the KC-46A tanker Lot 13 order in advance, as well as other seasonal working capital benefits in the quarter. As Robert said, we have increased clarity into our medium-term financial plan. In 2027, we expect to generate approximately $3 billion of free cash flow, followed by approximately $6 billion in 2028 and $10 billion in 2029, with significant growth potential beyond that in future years. For financial planning purposes, these targets assume that 777X will be certified by midyear 2027. For 2027, in addition to the absence of the DOJ payment

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: made in 2026, we expect free cash flow growth to be driven by higher commercial deliveries, modestly improved cash margins on the 737 and 787 programs, continued improvement at BDS, and continued steady growth at BGS. We expect these fundamental growth drivers to be partially offset by the impact of less favorable working capital, including lower year-over-year BCA order deposits, and around $1 billion of increased CapEx, which includes the growth associated with recent awards in BDS. Keep in mind, as we discussed earlier this year, 2027 free cash flow will be significantly impacted by the legacy cash drags. Beyond 2027, we expect these legacy cash drags to continue to abate, and the path to $10 billion to be underpinned by higher 737 and 787 deliveries with improving cash margins, positive cash contribution from 777X, profitable growth at BDS and BGS, and still-elevated but lower CapEx. As we have said before, there remains significant growth beyond $10 billion in the future. All of this is underwritten by the robustness and pricing included in our record backlog of $745 billion. As we advance, we would expect to provide additional assumptions in support of this free cash flow plan and other elements of the P&L. Summing it up, our focus remains on deliberate and disciplined execution, consisting of steady deliveries, validated rate step-ups, and operational performance that builds upon itself. We will not sacrifice long-term durability. Every decision is made to enable us

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: to deliver on the full potential of the business. With that, let's open up the line for questions.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: We will now begin the Q&A session. In the interest of time and to allow for broader participation, we ask that you limit yourself to one single-part question. Our first question comes from the line of Myles Walton from Wolfe Research. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Myles Walton, Analyst
passages.text: Myles Walton, Analyst: Thanks. Good morning, Jay. You went through a lot there on the walk from 2026 to 2027 free cash flow. A lot of positives, but yet it is only, excluding the DOJ payment, a few hundred million dollars of growth. Could you size the advances as being abnormal in 2027? And then maybe walk us a little bit more through the $3 billion expansion in 2028. Is that three quarters from 777X? Maybe just a combination of that and 2029. Thanks.

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: Okay, sure. Thanks, Myles. Let me maybe slow it down a little bit. I was moving pretty quickly there through the materials. Let me go back and give another quick summary here. As you mentioned, Myles, the DOJ payment does not repeat in 2027. That is a $700 million benefit. As I also said during my prepared remarks, we will get the benefit from BCA delivery volume, as well as modestly improving cash margins. You may recall, in the second quarter, I discussed BCA margins, and they were about breakeven for 2026. So our contribution from BCA will be largely from the improving cash margins in 2027. Of course, we will have continued growth from improvement at BDS and BGS. So those all taken together provide a positive benefit to cash flow in 2027. As you mentioned, and as I mentioned in my prepared remarks, we will expect to have lower customer deposits at BCA. 2026 was just a very strong year; it is trending to be a record year. The market is strong. Our campaign activity and pipelines remain robust. So we still expect 2027 order cash to be pretty strong as well, but just not at the same record level as 2026. I would size that in the range of a few billion dollars of impact. Then, as I mentioned, just to close it out, CapEx will be higher at $5 billion, so it is about $1 billion higher than 2026. Those are all the building blocks of 2027 free cash flow. As we get into 2028 and really 2029, it is kind of a

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: similar story. These legacy drags continue to abate and come down. We will see improving cash margins, and we will also get a higher benefit from higher delivery volumes because now we will be working from positive cash margins. So we will get a double benefit from both of those, and that is all supported by the backlog that we have. As we get to 2029 more specifically, we will be at higher production levels, and so I have said in the past that we expect the building blocks of $10 billion of free cash flow on a normalized basis to be around 52 on the 737 for deliveries, a delivery rate around 10 on the 787, and positive cash generation out of the 777 program. In 2029 specifically, we will be operating at higher production levels, which translate into higher delivery levels. We will be closer to the mid-to-high fifties on deliveries. In 2029, we will be closer to around 12 per month on the 787, and we will be generating, or expect to generate, positive free cash flow on the 777X in 2029. The reason we need to be at higher levels is because we will still have some residual drags in 2029. I expect those to be fully behind us for the most part by 2029. There is runway, as I mentioned in my prepared remarks, in 2030 and beyond above $10 billion. Hopefully, that encapsulates 2027 and also the future-year outlook for you.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: All right. Thank you, Jay. Your next question comes from the line of Seth Seifman from JPMorgan. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Seth Seifman, Analyst
passages.text: Seth Seifman, Analyst: Hey, thanks very much, and good morning. I wanted to ask a little bit about the unit returns on aircraft. You talked in the release about some cost growth that we are seeing. If you could give a little more color on what that is, both from the supply chain and from the process of increasing rates, and then also how it affects your thinking about unit cash profitability in the out-years. And then on the pricing side, the fact that we are looking at a more gradual ramp-up in rates, is that affecting the ability, or the timing, of moving beyond some of these legacy drags on unit revenue?

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: Seth, let me walk you through it. Let me start with the BCA margins here in the third quarter. I did talk about them being impacted by the rate adjustments, as well as higher supply chain costs. We had to roll those, as you know, through our EACs, which resulted in an impact to our booking rates. Specifically, I also had to talk about the 777 program, the existing freighter program, and the 767 program. We expect some abnormal costs to carry forward now in the fourth quarter and into the first half of the year. I expect those to put some pressure on third-quarter run-rate margins over that period of time, but they will abate and pretty much diminish in the second half of the year. When you take into account the benefit of cost-based extensions at a higher-priced backlog and other performance with the higher volumes, we will make some significant improvement in the back half of the year and put ourselves in a position to get to about breakeven in early 2028. As it relates to cash, all of this that we talked about, these impacts here in the third quarter, are all contemplated and factored into our cash flow projections, as well as the ramp in the cash margins over this period of time. I do not really see much of a difference there. We have absorbed it. We have contemplated that, and with the price mix already in the backlog, we are highly confident in the improving margin profile of the BCA programs, both

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Thank you. Your next question comes from the line of Sheila Kahyaoglu from Jefferies. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Sheila Kahyaoglu, Analyst
passages.text: Sheila Kahyaoglu, Analyst: Jay, Robert, thank you so much for all that long-term color, Robert. But maybe if we could just step back and talk about the macro. There is lots of interest around how higher-for-longer oil prices might affect the aerospace industry, and obviously you have a unique perspective on that. Can you maybe talk about customer channels you are checking to assess the market, whether it is orders, the services business, or just how you are seeing lease rates move around given the capacity cuts? And with your long-term guidance of free cash flow, what sort of oil price does that assume?

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: Yeah, Sheila. To confirm, we are in constant contact with all of our customers as we are navigating through these high fuel prices. I think the actual impact is going to be different depending on the airline. Obviously, a large portion of our backlog is going into replacement aircraft. For those customers who are bringing on new aircraft to replace older aircraft, these are much more fuel-efficient. In fact, the high fuel prices are driving them to really want these aircraft sooner. So the area where we may see softness is in overall growth, depending on what the airline's overall growth would be. So far, we have not seen that, Sheila. We have not seen anybody wanting to replan their order growth. If that should happen, quite frankly, given our oversold backlog, I think there is opportunity for us to shift around and manage through that. But obviously, it is something we have to keep an eye on. So far, the airlines have, for the most part, been flowing the higher fuel costs into ticket prices. I think over the next coming quarters, we will have to watch that. But again, at a macro level, I feel pretty good about our ability to manage even if we do see some softening demand in the growth market, because there are plenty of customers who are looking for airplanes faster for replacement. So we may have to rejigger a little bit of our firing order if that happens. It is not happening yet. We will just have to keep close

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: to our customers here.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Thank you. Your next question comes from the line of David Strauss from Wells Fargo. Your line is open.

passages.heading: David Strauss, Analyst
passages.text: David Strauss, Analyst: Thanks. Good morning, everyone.

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: Good morning.

passages.heading: David Strauss, Analyst
passages.text: David Strauss, Analyst: Jay, on the walk to 2027, can you maybe just put a finer point on what you are expecting for MAX and 787 deliveries, including what you are assuming for liquidation of the -7 and -10 inventory? And then, on 777X, I think that is obviously a pretty big timing risk item. If that slips out of 2027 into 2028, how much of a risk could that be to that $3 billion cash guide? Thanks.

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: Okay. Just on the inventory aircraft, next year we expect between the -7 and -10 to deliver around 30 aircraft that are prebuilt going into the year. On the 2027 cash bridge, what was the question on the 777?

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: He was asking about the 777, if it would slip out.

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: Oh, on the 777X program. Look, that is a scenario that would be significant. We are on a good path, though, as Robert mentioned during his prepared remarks. I think the risk would be more of a delay later in the year, which would have some impact on deliveries—about 10 to 15 deliveries next year, in that ballpark. Maybe you would see some deliveries come down a little bit. I think that could be absorbed within the $3 billion guide.

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: Yeah.

passages.heading: David Strauss, Analyst
passages.text: David Strauss, Analyst: And I was also hoping to get what you are exactly assuming for MAX deliveries and 787 deliveries in total next year.

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: Okay, yeah, that is the question I missed a piece of. We will give more color in January. What I can tell you is to think about total deliveries at BCA to be up 10% or more, similar to this year. We will give more color on that, more specifically by program, in January.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Scott Mikus from Melius Research. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Scott Mikus, Analyst
passages.text: Scott Mikus, Analyst: Good morning, Robert and Jay. Jay, I think you mentioned in the out-year 2029 timeframe that you are expecting 737 production in the mid-to-high fifties and 12 per month on the 787. You are going to be at 52 per month in the back half of next year on the 737 and moving to 10 per month on the 787 at the end of this year. I am just curious why it will take roughly two years to move up to those higher rates contemplated in the 2029 targets. Has the outlook for the supply chain deteriorated at all?

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: No, it is a good question. It is a very good question.

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: Typically, what we have is that deliveries do lag production. What I would characterize as the reconciliation of that is really the upside opportunity that we have in 2029. If we are able to deliver at these higher rates that we are producing at, then that would provide upside to the $10 billion target that we have out there.

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: Okay. Got it.

passages.heading: Scott Mikus, Analyst
passages.text: Scott Mikus, Analyst: And then, if I could just follow up real quick: any assumption on cash taxes or cash interest by the time you get to 2029?

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: It is more of the same. We will not start to have taxes kick in until the early 2030s. Cash interest will come down a little bit accordingly with the maturities, but not significant cash interest.

passages.heading: Scott Mikus, Analyst
passages.text: Scott Mikus, Analyst: Got it. Thank you.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Douglas Harned from Bernstein. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Doug Harned, Analyst
passages.text: Doug Harned, Analyst: Good morning. Thank you. Robert, if I go back to August, on the 737, we talked and things looked pretty stable at 47 a month, although, as you highlighted, there are wings, Wichita, engines, and all those things to think about. Engines, I think, seem fine. But in September, you described the challenges on drilling holes on the wing. As we look at getting the stability now, what has to happen? Is the wing issue resolved at this point? Where does Wichita stand? How do we get comfortable that, if the visibility was not that good back earlier in the summer, things are moving on the right track to get to 52 next year?

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: Yeah. Okay. So let me first of all say that engines are not a problem in this equation, so you can take that out of the equation. We had a series of flow enablers to allow us to ramp up production from 42 to 47, to support that in our wing back shop, or back shop. That is where we build all the wings for the 737 aircraft. Some of those flow enablers just flat out did not yield the flow savings. Some did, some did not. So we had to step back and make some changes to that. We have some additional flow enablers. In some cases, we are adding some capacity where we did not see the enablers yield, and we are going through that process right now. Early signs are encouraging. We are improving, but we are not yet to where I can say we are stably producing wings to support the 47-a-month rate. So we are going to want to dwell on that for a little while to make sure we are stable and do not end up in an unstable situation with production. That informs our next rate increase, obviously. We did not go as smoothly from 42 to 47 as we did from 38 to 42. We are going to want to make sure in the next rate break at 52 that we very much have understood and tested all of our rate-enabling functions in the back shops to make sure that they are going to yield. The other thing is, recognize that for rate 52, we have got to have the North Line up and running as well. Really no change to our outlook there; that is going well. In fact,

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: yesterday, we rolled out our first -10 from the Everett production facility. Look, we have to get wings stable, and that has been a challenge for us. It is just a result of the process improvement yields not being there. So what we are going to do is learn from that and make sure before we go to the next rate, we have fully tested these improvement areas and made sure that they are going to yield the next rate increase.

passages.heading: Doug Harned, Analyst
passages.text: Doug Harned, Analyst: But if I can, are there any other watch items here? In other words, if you get the wings stable and that is done, once that is done, things like fuselages coming out of Wichita and other supply chain questions—are there any other significant watch items, or will you feel pretty good about this once you have cleared the wing situation?

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: Well, I think right now wings are what have caused us the instability. Part of that is because we do have inventory in fuselages. But once we get through wings, fuselage will be an important focus area for us as well. Backing up on that, remember that we are producing fuselages at a lower rate than final assembly intentionally to burn down inventory. So the balance of this year and early into next year, we do have to see the ramp-up of fuselages also, and get synchronized with final assembly at rate 52. That is all in the calculus of our go-forward plan here: getting wings stable and ramping up the fuselage. I would not point you to anything else in the supply chain right now. There are always pop-up kinds of things, like we have had with the GKN windows, that we are working to alleviate. But there is no systemic challenge I see right now. Again, I think it is wings and fuselage that will be important for this next rate break.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Thank you. Your next question comes from the line of Peter Arment from Baird. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Peter Arment, Analyst
passages.text: Peter Arment, Analyst: Robert, you just touched upon Wichita a little bit, but maybe if you could just give us an update on the ongoing ramp we are seeing in Spirit. Any metrics you want to share on that progress? And then, Jay, just to confirm: BCA is cycling at much higher levels, and it sounds like you are calling out a potential breakeven margin in play for 2027. Are you expecting BCA margins to return to more historical levels with your 2029 outlook? Any color on the slope of the margin recovery at BCA would be helpful.

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: Okay. Let me start with Wichita. Overall, the integration is going according to our integration plan. One of the things that we were really focused on while we kept Wichita at a lower rate was implementing our safety and quality plan at Wichita that we were very successful in implementing in Renton, as you know. We have been doing that. I would say that has probably slowed them down a little bit as we have implemented some of these safety and quality features. You will see our inventory of fuselages is probably a little bit lower, or burning down a little bit faster, than what our baseline plan said. But again, we have got the ramp-up plans in place that are contemplated in our forecast here as we go forward. That is also contributing to making sure we stay stable at 47 a little bit longer before we move to 52.

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: And on the margin recovery, Peter, we often anchor and compare to 2018 margins. What I could say there is, on the 737, it will ramp up the margin profile, but will not reach what it was in 2018, either on a percentage or absolute basis. By contrast, the 787 by 2029 will exceed what it was in 2018, both on an absolute basis as well as on a percentage basis. Taken together, overall, it will be a net benefit.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: In 2029. Got it. That is helpful. Thank you. You are welcome. Your next question comes from the line of Noah Poponak from Goldman Sachs. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Noah Poponak, Analyst
passages.text: Noah Poponak, Analyst: Hey, good morning, guys.

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: Good morning.

passages.heading: Noah Poponak, Analyst
passages.text: Noah Poponak, Analyst: Jay, it seems like a decent amount of the variance in the free cash trajectory you just provided versus maybe what some people are thinking is CapEx. So you gave us 2027 CapEx. Maybe you could just give us the capital plan for 2028 and 2029, or when you get back to normalized as a percentage of revenue? And then on 777X, I guess it is fairly surprising to hear the answer to the prior question that you could absorb another slip. Last time it had to slip, everybody had to move free cash around a lot. So should we interpret that as you are providing conservative numbers you want to be able to beat, or is it just that the 777 delivery plan is so late in 2027 that it can slip?

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: Yeah. Let me address 777, and I will let Jesus talk about the cash flow. We did the reset last year, the last major reset on the 777 program. We definitely put management reserve in there to allow for additional schedule pressure going forward. I do not want to imply that the 777 program has moved to the middle of next year. We are still driving the team to certification. What we are saying is that we have financially provisioned such that if certification delays to the middle of the year, we will still be able to do that within our EAC. We are driving to a much earlier date right now. We do not yet, as I said in my prepared remarks, have full authorization for the flight-test program. There are a couple of things I will note. The FAA had a tremendous amount of work to do on the -7 and -10 certification, as did our test teams. Having that work behind us really does allow both parties to put more resources on the 777 test work that is yet ahead of us. I am hopeful to see us accelerate that as we run through the balance of the year and into next year. Airplanes are flying. We are making progress on the test program. We are getting some incremental authorization for additional flight testing from the FAA. Think of it as an extension to TIA 4B. We still have these big flight tests yet ahead of us, and flight-test authorizations yet ahead of us. We are working hard to get all that done. I will also say that I think we now

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: know, after the -7 and -10, what it takes to get certification complete in this new post-MAX world of regulation. That is factored into our planning, and we are executing that with the FAA now.

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: On your question, Noah, on CapEx: for 2027, about $5 billion, as I mentioned. 2028 and 2029 would be around $4 billion each year. Just circling back on the 777X cash question: again, it was in the context of the way Robert just laid it out. You are talking about an impact of a few months, a month or two, is what I was quantifying.

passages.heading: Noah Poponak, Analyst
passages.text: Noah Poponak, Analyst: And, Jay, going to $4 billion is still 3% of revenue. The company was running at 2%, or even a little below 2%, for a while. Is it structurally higher, or does that just have a lot of new projects and eventually work back down as a percentage of revenue?

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: Yeah. I would expect it to be higher than 2%. It will come down, I think, over time, but 3% to 4% is the right way to look at it on a normalized basis out in the future.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Okay. Thank you. Your next question comes from the line of John Godyn from Citi. Your line is open.

passages.heading: John Godyn, Analyst
passages.text: John Godyn, Analyst: Hey, guys. Thanks for taking my question. Robert and Jay, obviously, a lot of new detail about free cash flow for the next few years. If we took it at face value, it kind of seems like all the numbers are just sort of parallel shifting lower. What I want to ask about is just to make sure we have not lost sight of the North Star beyond 2029. Obviously, you do not have specific numbers out there. But if we thought about how our model should be changing in 2030 and 2031, or whenever you view getting past this period of ramp, has that ultimate number—the more full earnings power—changed in your mind? Has that North Star shifted at all? Any other color you are willing to give would be helpful.

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: I do not believe so. I think both Robert's comments and my comments said the same thing, which was that we expect significant growth beyond 2029. We will see continued runway on margin improvement, and that will be a continued source of increasing cash flow in addition to volumes. Back on the prior question, we were talking about what we are assuming for 2029 from a delivery perspective. That also provides runway to deliver at a rate of 63 on the 737 and at a rate of 14 on the 787. That will be a compounding benefit going beyond 2029.

passages.heading: John Godyn, Analyst
passages.text: John Godyn, Analyst: So is it fair to describe what is happening here as a steepening of the overall free cash flow profile, but getting to the same point?

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: You know, John, I kind of look at it as almost a one-year shift to the right from expectations. I do not think our expectations about the slope or the absolute endpoint have changed at all.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Appreciate that. Very clear. Thanks. Your next question comes from the line of Ronald Epstein from Bank of America. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Ron Epstein, Analyst
passages.text: Ron Epstein, Analyst: Robert and Jay, I promise I will not ask a cash flow question, but let's talk about something more fun. You guys won NGAD. You won F/A-XX. It would appear that the future of tactical military aviation for the U.S. is in Boeing's hands. So, Robert, how are you thinking about that for BDS? Should we think more broadly about BDS? How could BDS grow? What does that mean for margin? That is a real structural change, right? Just a couple of years ago, I do not think anybody thought that was in the cards. But here it is. How should we think about it?

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: Yeah. Well, first of all, we are going to see higher growth out of our defense portfolio than maybe what we thought a year ago. I think we were thinking more in terms of low-single-digit revenue growth. Clearly, that is going to be more towards the high-middle-single-digit or higher going forward. The important part is all these programs are also being underwritten with the right contract type. So not only are we booking more orders, we are booking more orders that will not result in some of the challenges we have had. And it is not just the order booking, Ronald. We have moved MQ-25. We have moved T-7 to Milestone C on both of those. A big new order on F-15EX, and there is more to come on that. The PAC-3 Seeker growth, and we have done MOUs with all of our customers on these big fixed-price development contracts. We have got Starliner under control here in the last quarter. So, look, I feel much, much better about both the growth profile and the margin performance profile. We still have to get through the development programs; we are not done with them until we are done. But Steve Parker and his team are doing a really, really good job of finding win scenarios with our customers to get these projects moving forward. The outlook is strong. Our products across the board are in strong demand, and the budget supports additional growth. I think our defense portfolio is a bit of a sleeper here.

passages.heading: Ron Epstein, Analyst
passages.text: Ron Epstein, Analyst: And just as a follow-up, to reiterate a question we get a lot, and this is for either of you: on F/A-XX or F-47, people ask whether it is fixed-price development. Can you give us a hint? Is it fixed price or not? I am hoping it is not. Can you give us a hint there?

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: The NGAD is cost-plus. For F/A-XX, I cannot say, but I will just say it is an appropriate contract type.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Thank you very much. Your next question comes from the line of Gavin Parsons from UBS. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Gavin Parsons, Analyst
passages.text: Gavin Parsons, Analyst: Thank you. Good morning. I was hoping to get your latest thoughts on the possibility of a new single-aisle aircraft and, separately, whether there is any assumption for higher R&D and CapEx related to that in the 2029 free cash flow guide. Thanks.

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: So really, nothing has changed in our outlook on a new airplane. We have a team working in our product development right now, trying to define what that looks like and what the market timing is. There is really no change in our outlook, and certainly any investment we need for that is contemplated in our cash outlook here.

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: Yeah, that is right. There are not significant types of investments here. More of our investments would be in R&D and technology development. We will be ramping down as we finish the 737 program—we are ramping down right now as we finish it. When we finish the 777 program, you will see a shift of resources and spending from those development programs to new programs.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Thank you. Your next question comes from the line of Gautam Khanna from TD Cowen. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Gautam Khanna, Analyst
passages.text: Gautam Khanna, Analyst: Yes. Good morning, guys. I was wondering if you could elaborate on the shape of deferred production across the three programs. Can you give us some sense for how much the balances will grow in aggregate next year, and then when they will decline and by how much in 2028 and 2029 in your assumptions? Thank you.

passages.heading: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: Jesus Malave Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer: Yeah, got it. I am not going to get into the specific changes, but what I will tell you is that on the 737 and 787, they essentially start to flatten out next year, so they are a lower use of cash. Going into 2028 and 2029, they become sources of cash. They become pretty significant sources of cash and drive working capital, and in total, continue to be a source of cash. I think those are directionally where they are going. The 777X program, because it is going to be early on in deliveries, will grow, and will grow over the next few years. But again, the cash drivers will be improved profitability on the 737 and 787 programs, and we will see a nice benefit from deferred production reductions on those two.

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: Operator, we have time for one more analyst question.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Certainly. Your final question comes from the line of Robert Stallard from Vertical Research Partners. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Robert Stallard, Analyst
passages.text: Robert Stallard, Analyst: Thanks so much. Good morning. Robert, maybe just to round things off here, I was wondering if you could comment on what has allowed you to give this free cash flow guidance. What has changed in terms of your outlook that gives you the confidence to give these numbers?

passages.heading: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Robert K. Ortberg, President and Chief Executive Officer: Yeah, Robert, look, it has been a couple of years of really taking challenges head-on and getting those challenges put to bed. We have significantly reduced the risk of this portfolio. If you look back just two years, every one of our fixed-price development programs was challenged. We have got that in hand. We did not know whether we would win any of the next-generation sixth-generation fighters. We have won both of those, so we have got that well in hand. We can see the improved performance in how we are underwriting our defense business. We also were, if you recall, two years ago, coming out of a strike and producing at zero in our commercial factories. We have successfully ramped up to 38, albeit the ramp to 47 has probably taken longer than anybody wants. Everybody wants us to go fast; I get that. But we are going to stay disciplined as we ramp up here. As we have looked at this, we feel like we have a better handle on the risk, to where we can provide you an outlook that we can meet. I think now is the time. The bar, as we said in our prepared remarks, is rising. We recognize that, and I think that is good. The expectations on ourselves are rising, too. We are providing this with confidence that the team is ready to execute. There are still things out there that we have to deal with, but not nearly the uncertainty we had before. I feel like it is a good time to do it.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: That is great. Thanks, Robert. That completes The Boeing Company's Third Quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. Thank you for joining.

# Boeing faces securities fraud probe after FAA delays 737 MAX 10

1 min read | Published on 12 Oct 2026, 03:14 AM |Updated on 12 Oct 2026

SEATTLE, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Boeing (BA.N) CEO Kelly Ortberg said on Tuesday that the company will miss its 737 production and jet delivery targets this year, dealing a setback ​to its recovery and sending shares tumbling nearly 10%, their worst day in more than 18 months.

The company also said it expects free cash flow to grow slower ‌than analysts expected, reaching its $10 billion target in 2029, a year later than investors' consensus, according to LSEG data.

The Misinformation Monitor newsletter rounds up international misinformation narratives, with a "Real or Fake?" quiz in every edition. Sign up here.

While many aerospace companies are struggling to increase output, Boeing is recovering from years of crises and controversies that dented its reputation, drained cash and saddled it with a heavy debt load.

That may make investors more inclined to sell shares, even though Boeing's long-term outlook remains good due to high demand for jetliners and only one major competitor, Europe's Airbus (AIR.PA), said Tony Bancroft, an investment analyst ​with Gabelli Funds investment group.

The market is going to punish any delay in increasing cash flow, he said.

Boeing expects to generate $3 billion next year, lower than Wall Street's consensus projection of $5.5 billion ​due to lower deliveries and higher capital investment, Jefferies analyst Sheila Kahyaoglu said in a research note on Tuesday.

The company posted free cash flow of $464 million ⁠in the most recent quarter; for the year so far it has burned through $359 million in cash, but it still expects to generate $2 billion by the end of the year.

Boeing reported an adjusted loss ​of 34 cents per share for the quarter through September, compared with an expected loss of 21 cents, according to data compiled by LSEG.

Shares were down 9.6% to $170.23 in afternoon trading, which would be the stock's ​worst day since April 3, 2025.

## PRODUCTION STRUGGLES

Boeing now expects to reach its 737 production rate target of 47 jets a month in early 2027. As recently as May, Boeing executives said they would hit that pace this summer.

As a result, Boeing will not reach its 500-jet delivery target this year, the company's financial chief Jay Malave said during a conference call with analysts on Tuesday.

Wing production continues to be a major constraint, but Boeing still plans to increase to 52 jets a ​month in the second half of 2027, Ortberg said on the call.

To reach that rate, Boeing needs to be producing five jets a month at its new 737 production line in Everett, Washington, which opened in ​July, and increase fuselage production at the former Spirit AeroSystems plant in Wichita, Kansas. Boeing bought Spirit last year in part due to significant ongoing manufacturing defects.

Currently, Boeing is making fuselages at a lower rate while it uses ‌up its existing ⁠inventory. Starting now, it has to increase output at Wichita to be in line with 737 output, Ortberg said.

Deliveries of the popular single-aisle jetliner are a major driver of Boeing's cash flow, and before Ortberg joined Boeing in 2024, the company had struggled for years with production problems due to rushing rate increases at the expense of quality.

Despite pressure to increase 737 output faster, "we're going to be smart about this, stay disciplined, and the outlook is there," Ortberg said.

The company continues to struggle with production challenges in its 787 program and a supplier dispute has stalled wing production for 777 freighters and 767s, which includes the KC-46 aerial ​refueling tanker, as first reported by Reuters on Friday.

Shipments ​for wing production have resumed, but the disruption ⁠will show up "over the next few quarters," Malave said.

Boeing expects the 777-9 jetliner will be on track for regulator certification by mid-2027, with 10 to 15 deliveries next year.

## LARGER-THAN-EXPECTED QUARTERLY LOSS

The dimmer outlook and a larger-than-expected quarterly loss overshadowed major wins by Boeing in recent months: certification by US regulators of the 737 MAX ​7 and MAX 10 and winning the US Navy's sixth-generation F/A-XX fighter contract.

"Expectations are rising, and they should. We have a stronger foundation than a year ago, ​but we also have more ⁠work to do to deliver on our backlog, strengthen our culture, and improve how we work every day," Ortberg said in a memo to employees after the results.

Revenue at Boeing's commercial airplanes division dipped slightly to $10.7 billion, while the operating loss stood at $697 million for an operating margin of negative 6.5%, compared with negative 48.3% a year ago.

The company attributed the performance to less profitable jetliner deliveries and higher production costs, including from its supply ⁠chain.

At Boeing's defense ​division, higher deliveries, improved operational performance and a $252-million sale of subsidiary HRL Laboratories contributed to nearly $500 million in quarterly earnings with ​an operating margin of 6.2%, up from 1.7% a year ago.

Boeing Global Services earned $1 billion and posted an operating margin of 18.3%.

The US planemaker ended the quarter with $25.2 billion in net debt, down slightly from $25.9 billion at the close of the previous quarter ​and $30.4 billion a year ago.

# Airbus holds annual targets, bets on year-end delivery surge

Reuters | Oct 29 2026 at 10:49 AM | [Air Cargo](https://www.ajot.com/news/channel/air-cargo "Air Cargo")

Airbus maintained its full-year forecasts and production plans on Wednesday after reporting mixed third-quarter earnings, leaving investors focused on whether it can hit its annual aircraft-delivery target.

The world's largest planemaker stuck to its target of delivering around 870 aircraft this year, which would be its highest tally ever, and left production goals unchanged. It will need a record fourth quarter to reach that mark.

"Everybody will be watching to see if they can get to that 870 number, or whether sometime in December, they need to indicate that they can't get to that number," said Ronan Murphy, a director at Alton Aviation Consultancy. "They must have a view that they can still get close to it."

Airbus said adjusted operating profit reached €1.77 billion ($2 billion) in the three months to end-September, broadly matching the analysts' estimate in a poll compiled by the company. Revenue fell 2% to €17.47 billion, below the estimate of €17.91 billion.

Airbus' American Depositary Receipts were trading up 1% following its earnings report.

RAM- UP SKEPTICISM

Airbus traditionally delivers more aircraft in the final months of the year, but has previously been forced to cut delivery targets late in the year as engine shortages and other supply-chain constraints disrupted production.

Airbus says those pressures have recently begun to ease.

"Two years ago we postponed part of the ramp-up and we progressed at a slower pace towards the ramp-up for a number of reasons, including the engines. "We are no longer in that situation," CEO Guillaume Faury told reporters.

The two separate quality flaws detected on some A321neo and A330 jetliners have been identified and contained, with deliveries still flowing, Faury added.

Murphy cautioned that supply-chain pressures had eased but not disappeared.

"The delays have slowed down, but there are still delays from when things were originally," said Murphy.

INVENTORY READY

Free cash flow before customer financing since January was a negative €1.27 billion, reflecting higher inventories as Airbus prepared for a stronger delivery performance later in the year and ramped up production for year-end deliveries.

"We are close to the end of October. We have a high level of inventory," Faury said, projecting confidence that Airbus will meet its delivery target this year.

Rival Boeing highlighted production delays and supply-chain challenges on Tuesday, with CEO Kelly Ortberg saying the US planemaker would miss key production and jet delivery targets this year.

Airbus remains ahead of its US rival in deliveries this year, having handed over 547 aircraft so far in 2026 compared with Boeing's 475.

"With current production rates, and Boeing pushing back its pace of rate breaks on the MAX, we believe there is growing skepticism on the airframers' abilities to hit production targets over the next 2 years," RBC analysts said.

# Airbus delivery slowdown squeezes profits, full-year target unchanged

[![Ian Molyneaux](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%2050%2050'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://www.aerotime.aero/articles/author/ian-molyneaux "View all posts by Ian Molyneaux")

[ByIan Molyneaux](https://www.aerotime.aero/articles/author/ian-molyneaux "View all posts by Ian Molyneaux")

Edited By [Emma Yates-Badley](https://www.aerotime.aero/articles/author/emmayatesbadley "Emma Yates-Badley")

2 minute read

 ![SWISS Airbus A350 900](https://www.aerotime.aero/images/2026/10/SWISS-Airbus-A350-900-800x533.jpg.webp "SWISS Airbus A350 900") 

SWISS

Airbus reported a decline in third-quarter profits, partly due to slower commercial aircraft deliveries; however, the planemaker left its full-year target unchanged.

On October 28, 2026, [Airbus](https://www.aerotime.aero/tag/airbus) delivered its nine-month and third quarter results, covering July to September 2026, when issues arose with both the A330neo and A321neo.

Airbus’ EBIT Adjusted figures for Q3 fell 9% compared with the same period last year, dropping to €1.77 billion ($1.97 billion) from €1.9 billion ($2.1 billion).

Airbus explained that the 9% decrease mainly reflected the “lower volume of commercial aircraft deliveries and a less favorable mix both at Commercial Aircraft and Airbus Helicopters, as well as the integration of the former Spirit AeroSystems work packages”.

| Month | Aircraft delivered | Running total |
| --- | --- | --- |
| January | 19 | 19 |
| February | 35 | 54 |
| March | 60 | 114 |
| April | 67 | 181 |
| May | 81 | 262 |
| June | 89 | 351 |
| July | 67 | 418 |
| August | 57 | 475 |
| September | 72 | 547 |
| Total (Jan–Sep) | 547 | 547 |

“Those were slightly offset by a stronger performance at Airbus Defence and Space,” Airbus said.

Q3 2026 revenues also decreased by 2%, which Airbus said mainly reflected the “lower volume of commercial aircraft deliveries partially offset by a higher services contribution”.

When only looking at Airbus’ commercial segment during Q3, EBIT Adjusted decreased by 12% from 2025.

In September 2026, Airbus delivered 72 commercial aircraft, while in August the company delivered 57 and in July, 67 were delivered.

## A330neo and A321neo issues

Airbus made no A330neo deliveries in June and July 2026, and only one, to Starlux Airlines, in August 2026, after a [quality issue affected production](https://www.aerotime.aero/articles/airbus-a330neo-tail-section-checks-stump-summer-deliveries-bloomberg).

In September 2026, Airbus also [identified a quality issue affecting A321neos](https://www.aerotime.aero/articles/airbus-says-a321neo-setback-is-quality-issue-not-a-safety-issue), which was subsequently contained.

Airbus’ nine-month EBIT Adjusted reflected more positively, showing an 8% increase from €4.1 billion ($4.56 billion) in 2025, to €4.49 billion ($5 billion) this year.

![A330neo first flight](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20683'%3E%3C/svg%3E "A330neo first flight")

Nine-month revenues increased 7% year-on-year to €50.6 billion ($56.3 billion) from €47.4 billion ($52.8 billion) in 2025.

“These nine-month results reflect the upward trajectory of our civil and military ramp-up, supported by strong demand for our products across the entire portfolio,” Airbus CEO Guillaume Faury said. “Against a complex geopolitical and operating environment, we are focused on delivery while maintaining a steadfast focus on quality. Our plan is clear, and our teams are onboard to meet our objectives.”

## 870 delivery target remains

Airbus also reaffirmed its ambition to deliver around 870 commercial aircraft in 2026.

Over the course of the year so far, Airbus has delivered 547 aircraft and therefore requires 323 further deliveries – around 108 per month.

Airbus has typically performed very strongly in the last three months of the year. Between October and December 2025, the company delivered 286 aircraft, including 136 in December alone.
